links.note: 1201 (the man, for Parimelazhagar) says love is sweeter than toddy because it gives great joy that does not end even when only thought of (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்). 1281, spoken by the woman, makes the same comparison: elation at a thought and delight at a sight belong to love and not to toddy (கள்ளுக்கு இல் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). The pairing shows the same judgment given from both sides of the couple, built on the same verb உள்ளுதல்.

1090 says brewed liquor gladdens only those who drink it (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது) and does not, like love, gladden those who merely see (கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று). 1201 moves the same contrast one step further from the senses: love gladdens even at a thought (உள்ளினும்), with nothing present to see. Read together they form a series from drinking to seeing to remembering.

Both verses turn on the word உள்ளினும். In 1201 the man says remembering gives unending joy (தீராப் பெருமகிழ்); in 1207 the woman says that even while she remembers, her heart burns (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the separation burning her despite the memory. These are two speakers in two moods, so it is a limit on the first claim and not a contradiction in the book's teaching.

1202 says love is sweet in every way since no pain comes from thinking of the one you love (நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல், as the commentators read this edition's garbled line). In 1209 the woman's dear life is wasting because she thinks hard on his lack of tenderness (அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து). The pairing shows that the sweetness of 1202 depends on what is remembered: the shared days, not the present neglect. Manakkudavar in fact reads 1202 as conditional, 'if no pain comes'.

1202 claims that thinking of the beloved brings no pain. In 1296 the woman says that when she sat alone and thought (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart stayed only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய); Parimelazhagar specifies that what she thought of was his cruelties. The two speeches mark out the cases in which remembering comforts and in which it wounds.

In 1203 a sneeze seems to start and dies away (தும்மல் சினைப்பது போன்று கெடும்), and the woman concludes he seemed about to think of her and did not. In 1317 the man sneezes and she weeps, asking whom he was thought of by (யாருள்ளித் தும்மினீர்). Both rest on the belief, noted by Parimelazhagar at 1203, that a sneeze means someone far away is thinking of you; the same sign feeds longing in separation and jealousy in union.

1203 uses the half-formed sneeze as a sign of the lover's half-formed thought of her. 1253 uses the sneeze differently: desire, though she would hide it, appears without her intending it, like a sneeze (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல் தோன்றி விடும்). In both the sneeze stands for what the will cannot command: in 1253 she cannot hold it back, in 1203 she cannot make it come.

1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). 1205 gives the answer as an accusation: he has put a guard on his heart against her (தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார்) and yet comes unceasingly into hers. Manakkudavar reads 1205 as the woman, having doubted, now deciding that he does not think of her.

In 1130 the woman answers the town's charge of lovelessness with the fact that he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்). In 1204 the same fact (எந்நெஞ்சத்து ஓஒ உளரே அவர்) no longer settles anything, because she now asks about his heart and not hers. The pairing shows that his presence in her heart is evidence only of her love.

1205 complains that he keeps her out of his heart while entering hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). 1291 states the same imbalance to her own heart: his heart stays his (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why is hers not hers? In 1205 she blames him for the unequal exchange, and in 1291 she blames her own heart.

Both verses treat the lover as physically lodged in her heart. In 1128 she fears to eat anything hot because he, being in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவர்), would be scalded; in 1205 the same lodger is an intruder who should be ashamed (நாணார்கொல்) to keep coming where he gives no entry in return. The image passes from tender care in the days of union to reproach in separation.

1206: she exists only by remembering the days she had with him (உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்), and asks what else she could live by. 1213: her life exists because she sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking (கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). Both make survival in separation depend on a mental substitute for his presence, memory by day and dream by night.

1206 says she lives by looking back at the days of union (உள்ள உளேன்). 1263 says she still lives by longing for his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). The same verb உளேன் is supported in one verse by the past and in the other by the expected future; Parimelazhagar on 1206 notes that the other supports, such as a messenger from him, are missing.

The two verses share the phrases மறப்பின் and மறப்பறியேன். In 1125 the man says he would remember her qualities only if he forgot them, and he does not know forgetting; in 1207 the woman, who also does not know forgetting, asks what would become of her if she did forget, when even remembering burns. The man's unforgetting is offered as proof of love, and the woman's as a pain she still prefers to the alternative.

In both verses the woman rejects the idea of forgetting him, which Parimelazhagar says the friend had advised in each case. 1207 asks what she would become if she forgot (மறப்பின் எவனாவன்); 1262 answers concretely that if she forgot today (இன்று மறப்பின்) her beauty would go and the bangles slip from her arms. Remembering hurts, but both verses hold that forgetting would be worse.

1207 says that even as she remembers, her heart is burned (உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1159 describes the same burning as a property of love's sickness: fire burns only when touched, and cannot burn when one moves away as love does (விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ). 1159 gives the general paradox of a fire that burns at a distance, and 1207 shows it at work inside memory.

The verses share the words நினை and காய். In 1208 the woman says that however much she thinks of him he is not angry (எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார்), and that this is all the honour he does her. In 1320 the man reports that when he merely sits thinking and looks at her she is angry (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும்) and asks whom he is thinking of. The absent lover tolerates everything because he is not there to care, while the present one is questioned about every thought.

1199 says that though the one she longs for gives nothing (நல்கார் எனினும்), even a word about him is sweet to her ear. 1208 measures what an ungiving lover leaves her more sharply: his whole gift (சிறப்பு) is that he does not object to being thought of. Parimelazhagar takes 1208 as scorn of the friend's promise that he will come and be kind, whereas Manakkudavar takes the not-being-angry as real grace.

In 1122 the man says the bond between him and her is like that between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை). In 1209 the woman recalls him as the one who used to say 'we are not separate' (வேறல்லம் என்பார்) and says her sweet life is perishing (விளியுமென் இன்னுயிர்) as she thinks on his lack of tenderness. His figure of body and life is taken literally in her speech: with him gone, the life is leaving.

Both verses hold the lover to his earlier words. 1154 asks whether any fault lies with those who trusted the assurance of the one who was tender and said 'do not fear' (அளித்தஞ்சல் என்றவர்), if he then leaves. 1209 sets his saying 'we are not separate' against his present அளியின்மை, the absence of that same அளி. Parimelazhagar notes at 1209 that she says her life is going not because of the parting but because of his lovelessness.

Both verses address the moon and close with the same words, வாழி மதி. In 1118 the man tells the moon it could be loved if it shone like her face; in 1210 the woman asks the moon not to set (படாஅதி), so that she may see with her eyes the man who went without leaving her heart. The man treats the moon as a rival to her face and the woman treats it as a way to reach him.

1170 says that if her eyes could go where he is, as her mind does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in tears. 1210 looks for a way round that limit: on Parimelazhagar's reading, since both of them look at the moon, her eyes meet his there (கண்ணினால் காண). Manakkudavar reads it differently, as a complaint that the moon will not set and let her sleep and see him in a dream.

Both verses end on the word விருந்து, a feast. In 1211 the woman (for Parimelazhagar) asks what feast she can make for the dream that came bringing her lover's messenger (யாதுசெய் வேன்கொல் விருந்து). In 1268 the man, away on the king's work, looks forward to the evening feast at home once the king has won (மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து). The real feast waits on his return, and meanwhile she can offer hospitality only to a dream.

In 1211 the dream arrives as the carrier of his message (காதலர் தூதொடு வந்த கனவு). In 1212 she wants to use the dream in the other direction: if her eyes would sleep, she would herself declare to him that she survives (உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன்). Parimelazhagar says this is spoken when she was thinking of sending a messenger, and that she would tell him in full what she would hold back from one.

1212 makes everything depend on a condition: if her eyes would sleep when she begs them (யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சின்). 1179 says why the condition fails: her eyes do not sleep when he does not come and do not sleep when he does (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா). Set beside chapter 122, this shows that the dream which consoles her in the following verses is not available to her at will.

1162 says she cannot hide this sickness, and telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்); Parimelazhagar takes the telling there to mean sending a messenger. In 1212 she is ready to proclaim her state to him herself (சாற்றுவேன்), but only in a dream. The shame that blocks the message in waking life does not apply to speech in a dream.

1198 says no one in the world is harder than those who go on living without getting even a kind word from the one they love (வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்). 1213 has the woman living on though he gives her nothing in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை), and explains it: her life exists because she sees him in dreams (கனவினால் காண்டலின்). The second verse answers the first's charge of hardness by naming what keeps her alive.

1170 regrets that her eyes cannot travel to where he is as her mind can. In 1214 the dream does the travelling: it seeks out the man who gives nothing in waking life and brings him (நல்காரை நாடித் தரற்கு), and so there is pleasure in the dream. Parimelazhagar spells it out: the dream goes to the country he went to, finds him and delivers him.

1201 says love gives a joy that does not end even in recollection (உள்ளினும் தீரா). 1215 says that what she saw in waking was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet just while it is seen (கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது). Manakkudavar glosses both pleasures as lasting for that moment; Parimelazhagar takes her point to be that dream and waking are therefore equal for her. On either reading the woman's sweetness is tied to the moment of seeing, where the man's persists in thought.

In 1216 the woman says that if there were no such thing as waking, her lover would not leave her in the dream (கனவினால் காதலர் நீங்கலர் மன்). In 1329 the man, in the middle of a lovers' quarrel, wishes the night would lengthen so that he can go on pleading (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா). Both wish away the end of the night and both close on the wistful particle மன்; hers is said of a dream meeting and his of a real one.

1169 calls the long nights of separation crueller than the cruel man himself (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1216 wants the night's state never to end, with waking itself abolished (நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின்). The difference is sleep: the night is an enemy when she lies awake and a refuge when it brings the dream, and Parimelazhagar accordingly has her call waking a villain (பாவி).

The two verses open with nearly the same words, நனவினால் நல்காதவரை and நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார், and reach opposite verdicts on the dream. In 1213 seeing him in dreams keeps her alive; in 1217 she asks why the cruel one torments her in dreams (எம்மைப் பீழிப்பது). Parimelazhagar places 1217 after she has woken and found him gone, so the dream comforts while it lasts and wounds once it has ended.

819, on bad friendship, says the tie with those whose deeds are one thing and words another is bitter even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). In 1217 the lover who gives nothing in waking life hurts her in her dreams as well (கனவினால் ... பீழிப்பது). Both take the dream as the last place a person's unreliability should reach, and both find that it reaches there: one verse in the book of polity, the other in a lover's complaint.

Both verses describe the same event: he is with her in sleep and gone on waking. In 1217 this is his cruelty; Parimelazhagar explains the torment as his being on her shoulder in the dream and vanishing when she wakes. In 1218 she tells it in his favour: asleep he is on her shoulder (தோள்மேலர்), and awake he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து), so he never leaves her at all. Parimelazhagar says 1218 is her defence of him after the friend had spoken against him.

1218 says that on waking he quickly becomes one who is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர்). 1249 tells her own heart that the lover is inside it (உள்ளத்தார் காதலவர்), so there is no one to go out looking for. Both use his dwelling in her heart to deny that he is absent; 1218 adds the dream so that both night and day are covered.

The two verses have the same construction: an opinion is held only by those who lack an experience. In 66, 'the flute is sweet, the lute is sweet' is said by those who have not heard their own children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல் கேளாதவர்). In 1219 those who blame the man for giving nothing in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (கனவினால் காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Parental love in the first book and a lover's dream in the third both discredit a judgment by pointing to what its holders have not known.

In 1140 the woman says the ignorant laugh in her sight because they have not suffered what she has (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு). In 1219 others blame her lover because they have never seen a lover in dreams. In both she rejects outsiders' judgment of her love on the ground that they lack her experience; in 1140 what they lack is her suffering, in 1219 her consolation.

1236: with bangles and arms slackening, what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). 1219 goes from that pain to a rebuttal: those who blame him (நோவர்) are people who have not seen a lover in their dreams. Parimelazhagar gives both verses the same occasion, the friend speaking ill of the man, and says she puts her reply in 1219 on strangers out of displeasure with the friend.

Both verses set the town (இவ்வூர்) against the woman's private evidence. In 1130 the town says he is loveless and lives apart, while he lives gladly in her heart always; in 1220 the townspeople say he has left her in waking life (நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார்), and she asks whether they do not see him in dreams. The town's report is confined to what can be observed, and she appeals each time to something only she can witness.

In 1188 the woman complains that people only say 'she has gone pale' and no one says 'he has abandoned her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1220 the townspeople do say he has left her (நம்நீத்தார் என்பர்) and she objects to it. The conflict holds only if 1188 is read as her wanting the blame to fall on him, and both are speeches of a moment, not doctrine: she resents his being excused and resents his being accused.
